It's a fair reading of the API, and simple experiments seem to confirm it. Log something after a
and the log appears first, then

runs a moment later, which looks like "right after". Tutorials often describe the trick as "defer until the call stack is clear", and that's half of the truth. The missing half is that the event loop has more than one queue, and promise callbacks wait in a queue that always goes first.
One thread, and every job runs to completion

Your page's JavaScript runs on one thread, one job at a time. MDN's execution model calls this run-to-completion: once a job starts, it can't be preempted, and nothing else runs until the call stack is empty. A script, a click handler and a timer callback are each a job that finishes before the next one begins. So
can never interrupt the code that called it, whatever the delay.

once 0 ms have passed. MDN puts it precisely: a delay of 0 runs in the next event cycle, not immediately. Even "next" isn't promised: the HTML Standard gives the event loop several task queues and lets the browser choose which one to serve, so a click that arrives after your timer can still run before it.
Microtasks: the queue that always goes first
Promise callbacks don't become tasks. The HTML Standard schedules promise jobs in the
. After every task, the event loop performs a microtask checkpoint, which runs microtasks until the queue is empty, including the ones queued along the way. Only then does it move on.

Node 24 prints the five lines in numeric order, and the HTML Standard's processing model gives browsers the same order: the synchronous code finishes, both microtasks run (the second one was queued while the first ran), and only then does the timer's task get its turn. The timer was scheduled first and still runs last.
Between tasks, a browser may update the rendering: run

callbacks, recalculate styles and layout, and paint. It never does this in the middle of a task or while microtasks are pending, and it doesn't have to do it after every task: the spec explicitly allows a browser to run several timer callbacks back to back with no rendering in between. So

content.text: A 0 ms timer can wait much longer. The HTML Standard clamps nested timers: once timers have nested more than five levels deep, delays under 4 ms become 4 ms. Browsers also throttle timers in background tabs; MDN notes that desktop Firefox enforces a minimum of 1 second there. Never use a timer as a "soon" signal when a microtask says what you mean.

The checkpoint runs until the microtask queue is empty, so a microtask that keeps queuing microtasks never lets the loop move on: no timers, no input events, no rendering. A recursive promise chain, or an

After every task, all microtasks (promise callbacks, code after
) run before the next task, including the ones queued meanwhile.
The browser chooses among task queues and may render between tasks, but never while microtasks are pending.
"0 ms" can mean 4 ms or a full second: nested timers are clamped and background tabs are throttled.
When your code depends on an order, make it explicit instead of betting on which queue wins.
